linkedin:
A plain QR code is just a URL. Anyone with a printer can make one that looks identical to yours and points somewhere else.

QRON signs the payload instead. The data in the code carries an Ed25519 signature, so a verifier can check that the content wasn't altered and which key signed it, rather than trusting whatever the code happens to point at.

The honest boundary: a valid signature proves integrity and issuer-key control. It does not prove that the label on the box in front of you is the one the signature was issued for, because a genuine code can still be copied onto another item. That is why signed codes work best alongside registry and scan-pattern checks, and QRON treats the signature as one layer, not a verdict.

A code can also be printed with a higher error-correction level (L, M, Q or H) so it stays readable when a label is scuffed or partly covered.

If you print codes on products, packaging or documents, what do you check when someone scans one?

reddit.title: A QR code is just a URL anyone can reprint. We sign the payload (Ed25519) so a scanner can check it. What are we missing?
reddit.body:
QRON generates QR codes whose payload carries an Ed25519 signature, so a verifier can check that the content wasn't altered and which key signed it, instead of trusting wherever the code points.

The limits, stated plainly: a valid signature proves payload integrity and issuer-key control. It does not prove the physical label is the one the signature was issued for. A genuine signed code can be copied onto another item, so we treat the signature as one layer next to registry and scan-pattern checks. Ed25519 is also not quantum-safe.

Question for people who deal with QR codes in production: what do you actually verify when a code is scanned, and where do signed payloads get in your way (scanner support, payload size, key rotation)?
